summarize this text: Speaking at a press conference after the second shooting, President Aleksandar Vucic announced a push to disarm the country as he condemned the latest attack as "terrorism" and "an attack on us all".

Serbia has among the highest firearm ownership rates in the world, and he said no new gun permits would be issued.

"We will conduct a revision of all people who posses firearms, around 400,000 of them. After these checks, there will be no more than 30,000 to 40,000 weapons legally owned," he said.

He also announced that penalties for illegal possession of firearms will be doubled. Penalties for carrying weapons like knives will be increased as well.

Weapons holders will be subjected to more frequent psychiatric and psychological tests, as well as ad hoc drug testing.

President Vucic also vowed to strengthen security for schools, announcing that 1,200 new police officers will be recruited in the next six months to be deployed to schools across the country.

Mass shootings are extremely rare in Serbia, although gun ownership in the country is among the highest in Europe.

The western Balkans are also awash with illegal weapons following wars and unrest in the 1990s. In 2019, it was estimated that there are 39.1 firearms per 100 people in Serbia - the third highest in the world, behind the US and Montenegro.
response: President Aleksandar Vucic of Serbia announced a comprehensive plan to reduce the country's high firearm ownership rates following a shooting incident. He condemned the attack as "terrorism" and vowed to conduct a thorough review of all firearm owners, reducing the number of legally owned weapons from around 400,000 to between 30,000 and 40,000. The president also stated that no new gun permits would be issued and that penalties for illegal firearm possession would be doubled, with similar increases for carrying knives. Additionally, weapons holders will face more frequent psychiatric and psychological evaluations and drug tests. To enhance school security, Vucic pledged to recruit 1,200 new police officers over the next six months. Serbia, despite having one of the highest firearm ownership rates in Europe, rarely experiences mass shootings. The country's high weapon prevalence is attributed to the aftermath of the 1990s wars and unrest in the western Balkans.
